FP511 MCQ Practice — CFP Study Lab
==================================
FP511 — General Financial Planning, Conduct & Psychology
===== FP511 MCQ PRACTICE =====

Read the question and options, commit to an answer, then turn the page for the correct choice, the explanation, and why each wrong option is wrong.
50 questions · 5 sections.



===== FP511 · M1 PERSONAL FINANCIAL PLANNING =====

[9 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 9 · Disclosure method]
Which disclosure may be delivered either verbally OR in writing in both Financial Advice and Financial Planning engagements?
A. Privacy policy
B. Public discipline and bankruptcy
C. How the firm and related parties are compensated
D. Material conflicts of interest
Answer: D. Material conflicts of interest
Material conflicts of interest may be delivered verbally or in writing. Privacy policy, compensation, and public discipline/bankruptcy must be in writing.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Privacy policy — The privacy policy must be delivered in writing, not verbally.
✗ Public discipline and bankruptcy — Public discipline and bankruptcy disclosures must be in writing.
✗ How the firm and related parties are compensated — Compensation disclosure must be in writing, not merely verbal.

——————————
[Q 2 / 9 · Documentation methods]
According to the Practice Standards, all of the following are approved documentation methods EXCEPT:
A. CRM software
B. Voice memos
C. Handwritten notes
D. Emails
Answer: B. Voice memos
Approved methods are CRM software, handwritten notes, and emails. Voice memos are not listed as an approved method.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ CRM software — CRM software is an approved documentation method, so it is not the exception.
✗ Handwritten notes — Handwritten notes are an approved documentation method.
✗ Emails — Emails are an approved documentation method; voice memos are the one not listed.

——————————
[Q 3 / 9 · Qualitative data]
In data gathering, which of the following is QUALITATIVE (subjective) rather than quantitative data?
A. Section 401(k) account statement
B. Income tax return
C. Personal goals and objectives
D. Liability/debt statement
Answer: C. Personal goals and objectives
Personal goals and objectives are qualitative (subjective) data. Account statements, tax returns, and debt statements are quantitative (objective) data.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Section 401(k) account statement — An account statement is hard, objective (quantitative) data, not subjective.
✗ Income tax return — A tax return is objective quantitative data — numbers and facts, not subjective.
✗ Liability/debt statement — A debt statement is quantitative (objective) data, not qualitative.

——————————
[Q 4 / 9 · Incomplete information]
If a planner cannot obtain sufficient and relevant quantitative information to form a basis for recommendations, the planner must:
A. Proceed using reasonable assumptions for the missing data
B. Either restrict the scope of the engagement or terminate it
C. Report the client to CFP Board
D. Obtain the information from a third party without client consent
Answer: B. Either restrict the scope of the engagement or terminate it
Per Step 1, the planner must either restrict the scope to matters with sufficient information or terminate the engagement, and communicate any scope limitations to the client.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Proceed using reasonable assumptions for the missing data — You can't fabricate a basis with assumptions for missing core data; you must restrict scope or terminate.
✗ Report the client to CFP Board — A client withholding information is not a reportable violation; the planner restricts scope or terminates.
✗ Obtain the information from a third party without client consent — Gathering data without client consent breaches confidentiality; the fix is to limit scope or terminate.

——————————
[Q 5 / 9 · Implementation responsibility]
Under Code & Standards A.10.b.ii, who is responsible for implementing Financial Planning recommendations?
A. The client, always
B. The planner, unless specifically excluded from the Scope of Engagement
C. A third-party custodian
D. CFP Board
Answer: B. The planner, unless specifically excluded from the Scope of Engagement
The planner is responsible for implementing the recommendations unless specifically excluded from the Scope of Engagement; the client accepts or rejects the recommendations.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ The client, always — Not always the client — the planner is responsible unless specifically excluded from the Scope of Engagement.
✗ A third-party custodian — A custodian merely holds assets; implementation responsibility rests with the planner unless scoped out.
✗ CFP Board — The CFP Board sets standards; it never implements client recommendations.

——————————
[Q 6 / 9 · Fee-only]
A firm receives only financial planning fees and no commissions or sales-related compensation. Under Standard A.12, this firm is:
A. Fee-based
B. Fee-only
C. Commission-based
D. Fee-offset
Answer: B. Fee-only
Fee-only means the firm receives only planning fees. Fee-based means planning fees plus commissions/sales-related compensation.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Fee-based — Fee-based requires commissions/sales compensation ADDED to fees; this firm takes fees only, so it's fee-only.
✗ Commission-based — The firm earns no commissions at all, so it cannot be commission-based.
✗ Fee-offset — Fee-offset reduces fees by commissions earned — but this firm earns no commissions, so the term doesn't apply.

——————————
[Q 7 / 9 · 7-step order]
Which correctly orders steps 4 through 6 of the Financial Planning Process?
A. Developing → Implementing → Presenting
B. Developing → Presenting → Implementing
C. Presenting → Developing → Implementing
D. Implementing → Developing → Presenting
Answer: B. Developing → Presenting → Implementing
Step 4 Developing, Step 5 Presenting, Step 6 Implementing recommendations (then Step 7 Monitoring).
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Developing → Implementing → Presenting — Presenting (Step 5) comes before Implementing (Step 6), not after.
✗ Presenting → Developing → Implementing — Developing (Step 4) precedes Presenting (Step 5); this reverses the first two.
✗ Implementing → Developing → Presenting — Implementing is Step 6, not first — order is Develop, Present, Implement.

——————————
[Q 8 / 9 · Marks usage]
Which is a CORRECT use of the CFP® marks?
A. John Doe, C.F.P.
B. John Doe, a CFP
C. John Doe, CFP®
D. John Doe, cfp
Answer: C. John Doe, CFP®
The marks use capital letters, no periods, and the ® symbol. "John Doe, CFP®" is correct; periods and a missing ® are incorrect.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ John Doe, C.F.P. — Periods are not permitted — the marks use no periods and require the ® symbol.
✗ John Doe, a CFP — The marks may not be used as a noun and must include the ® symbol.
✗ John Doe, cfp — Lowercase is incorrect — the marks require capital letters and the ® symbol.

——————————
[Q 9 / 9 · Life cycle phase]
A 70-year-old retiree making lifetime gifts to heirs and executing estate strategies is primarily in which financial life-cycle phase?
A. Asset accumulation
B. Conservation/protection
C. Distribution/gifting
D. Liquidation
Answer: C. Distribution/gifting
The distribution/gifting phase runs roughly from retirement (~age 60) to death and features gifting and estate planning.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Asset accumulation — Accumulation is the early wealth-building phase, not the retiree gifting/estate stage.
✗ Conservation/protection — The conservation phase focuses on protecting and growing assets pre-retirement, before active gifting.
✗ Liquidation — Liquidation is not a standard named life-cycle phase; retirement gifting is the distribution/gifting phase.



===== FP511 · M2 PSYCHOLOGY OF FINANCIAL PLANNING =====

[12 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 12 · Loss aversion]
An investor refuses to sell a losing stock, waiting to "get even," even though better opportunities exist. This best illustrates:
A. Anchoring
B. Loss aversion
C. Confirmation bias
D. Mental accounting
Answer: B. Loss aversion
Loss aversion is the tendency to fear losses more than valuing equivalent gains, causing reluctance to realize losses ("get-even-itis").
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Anchoring — That's fixating on a reference price generally; the core driver here is fearing the loss (loss aversion).
✗ Confirmation bias — That's seeking info that supports a belief, not the emotional refusal to realize a loss.
✗ Mental accounting — That's siloing money by purpose, not the aversion to taking a loss on this position.

——————————
[Q 2 / 12 · Cognitive vs emotional]
How should a planner generally handle a purely EMOTIONAL bias, as compared with a cognitive bias?
A. Correct it with more information and education
B. Ignore it
C. Accommodate it, since it is harder to overcome
D. Report it to a compliance officer
Answer: C. Accommodate it, since it is harder to overcome
Cognitive biases can often be corrected with information; emotional biases are harder to overcome and may need to be accommodated.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Correct it with more information and education — That's how you handle a cognitive bias; emotional biases resist information and usually must be accommodated.
✗ Ignore it — Biases affecting decisions can't be ignored; emotional ones should be accommodated in the plan.
✗ Report it to a compliance officer — A behavioral bias isn't a compliance violation; it's addressed through counseling, not reporting.

——————————
[Q 3 / 12 · Confirmation bias]
A client overloads on employer stock and only reads news supporting that decision. This reflects:
A. Recency bias
B. Confirmation bias
C. Status quo bias
D. Endowment bias
Answer: B. Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is seeking or distorting information to support an existing view, often leading to under-diversification in employer stock.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Recency bias — That's overweighting recent events, not selectively seeking info that supports holding employer stock.
✗ Status quo bias — That's preferring the existing state/inaction, not actively filtering for confirming information.
✗ Endowment bias — That's overvaluing what you own; here the tell is seeking only supportive news (confirmation bias).

——————————
[Q 4 / 12 · Mental accounting]
A client refuses to use money set aside in a "vacation fund" to repair a leaking roof and instead pays penalties to borrow elsewhere. This is:
A. Mental accounting
B. Framing bias
C. Self-control bias
D. Affinity bias
Answer: A. Mental accounting
Mental accounting (money jar mentality) treats funds differently by purpose, sometimes irrationally.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Framing bias — That's deciding differently based on how a choice is worded, not siloing money into purpose-based jars.
✗ Self-control bias — That's failing to act in one's long-term interest from lack of discipline, not compartmentalizing funds.
✗ Affinity bias — That's investing to reflect one's identity/values, not treating earmarked funds as untouchable.

——————————
[Q 5 / 12 · Status quo / defaults]
Automatic enrollment in a retirement plan leverages which behavioral tendency to improve participation?
A. Overconfidence
B. Status quo bias
C. Loss aversion
D. Representativeness
Answer: B. Status quo bias
Status quo bias is comfort with the existing situation; defaults and automatic enrollment use this tendency to keep participants saving.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Overconfidence — That's overrating one's own judgment; defaults work by exploiting inertia, not confidence.
✗ Loss aversion — That's fearing losses more than valuing gains; auto-enrollment works via inertia/status quo, not loss framing.
✗ Representativeness — That's judging by stereotypes/resemblance, not the tendency to stick with a default option.

——————————
[Q 6 / 12 · Risk capacity]
The degree to which a client's financial resources can absorb and mitigate risk is the client's:
A. Risk tolerance
B. Risk perception
C. Risk capacity
D. Risk preference
Answer: C. Risk capacity
Risk capacity refers to financial resources' ability to mitigate risk; risk tolerance is the willingness to accept risk.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Risk tolerance — That's the willingness (subjective) to accept risk, not the objective resource ability to absorb it.
✗ Risk perception — That's how risky the client feels something is, not the financial ability to absorb risk.
✗ Risk preference — That's a stated liking for more or less risk, not the resources available to absorb it.

——————————
[Q 7 / 12 · Money scripts]
Unconscious money beliefs formed in childhood that are resistant to change are called:
A. Money scripts
B. Mental accounts
C. Money illusions
D. Financial comfort zones
Answer: A. Money scripts
Money scripts are unconscious, often childhood-formed attitudes about money that resist change.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Mental accounts — Those are purpose-based mental “jars” for money, not deep-seated childhood money beliefs.
✗ Money illusions — That's confusing nominal and real dollars, not unconscious childhood-formed money attitudes.
✗ Financial comfort zones — Not the standard term; the childhood-rooted, resistant beliefs are money scripts.

——————————
[Q 8 / 12 · Financial therapy referral]
A client shows signs of a compulsive-buying disorder affecting their finances. The CFP® professional should:
A. Provide therapy personally
B. Refer the client to a financial therapist / licensed mental health professional
C. Terminate the relationship immediately
D. Ignore it as outside financial planning
Answer: B. Refer the client to a financial therapist / licensed mental health professional
Serious psychological/pathological money issues should be referred to a financial therapist or licensed mental health professional; planner involvement in feelings should stay general and limited.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Provide therapy personally — Planners aren't licensed therapists; providing therapy exceeds their competence and role.
✗ Terminate the relationship immediately — Abandoning the client isn't appropriate; the proper step is referral to a mental health professional.
✗ Ignore it as outside financial planning — It materially affects finances and can't be ignored; refer to a financial therapist/mental health professional.

——————————
[Q 9 / 12 · Social Penetration]
In Social Penetration Theory, the stage marked by significant trust, open disclosure, and intimacy is:
A. Orientation
B. Exploration
C. Affective Exchange
D. Stable Exchange
Answer: C. Affective Exchange
Affective Exchange features significant trust and open disclosure. Stable Exchange is the deepest, established long-term pattern.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Orientation — That's the first-meeting, general-conversation stage — well before significant trust develops.
✗ Exploration — That's a middle stage of increasing but still limited sharing, not deep trust and open disclosure.
✗ Stable Exchange — That's the deepest, established long-term pattern; the stage first marked by significant trust/open disclosure is Affective Exchange.

——————————
[Q 10 / 12 · Profiling questions]
For effective psychological profiling and goal discovery, a planner should primarily use:
A. Closed-ended yes/no questions
B. Open-ended questions
C. Leading multiple-choice prompts
D. Standardized forms only
Answer: B. Open-ended questions
Open-ended questions prompt clients to answer in their own words, yielding richer profiling information.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Closed-ended yes/no questions — These limit answers to yes/no and yield thin information, poor for rich profiling.
✗ Leading multiple-choice prompts — Leading prompts steer the client and bias answers, undermining genuine discovery.
✗ Standardized forms only — Forms alone can't capture the client's own words and nuance needed for profiling.

——————————
[Q 11 / 12 · Cultural humility]
A planner's lifelong process of self-evaluating their own beliefs and assumptions about other cultures is:
A. Cultural competency
B. Cultural humility
C. Cultural framing
D. Affinity awareness
Answer: B. Cultural humility
Cultural humility is the ongoing self-evaluation of one's beliefs; cultural competency alone (learned knowledge) can lead to cultural bias.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Cultural competency — That's acquired knowledge about cultures; relied on alone it can breed cultural bias. The ongoing self-evaluation is cultural humility.
✗ Cultural framing — Not the standard term; the lifelong self-reflection process is cultural humility.
✗ Affinity awareness — Not the standard term; the ongoing self-examination of one's own cultural assumptions is cultural humility.

——————————
[Q 12 / 12 · Endowment bias]
A client demands far more to sell an inherited stock than she would ever pay to buy it. This best illustrates:
A. Endowment bias
B. Anchoring
C. Recency bias
D. Framing bias
Answer: A. Endowment bias
Endowment bias is overvaluing an asset simply because one owns it, so the selling price exceeds the buying price.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Anchoring — That's fixating on a reference number; the gap here comes from overvaluing what she owns (endowment).
✗ Recency bias — That's overweighting recent events, not valuing an asset more simply because she owns it.
✗ Framing bias — That's deciding differently based on wording, not the ownership-driven sell-vs-buy price gap.



===== FP511 · M3 FINANCIAL STATEMENTS & CASH FLOW =====

[17 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 17 · FDIC limit]
What is the basic FDIC insured amount, per depositor, per ownership category, per institution?
A. $100,000
B. $250,000
C. $500,000
D. Unlimited
Answer: B. $250,000
FDIC insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per ownership category, per insured institution; credit unions are insured to the same limit by the NCUA.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ $100,000 — $100,000 was the old pre-2008 limit; the current FDIC limit is $250,000.
✗ $500,000 — $500,000 is the SIPC securities limit, not the FDIC deposit limit of $250,000.
✗ Unlimited — FDIC coverage is capped at $250,000 per depositor, per ownership category, per institution — not unlimited.

——————————
[Q 2 / 17 · FDIC coverage scope]
Which of the following is NOT covered by FDIC insurance?
A. A certificate of deposit (CD)
B. A savings account
C. Shares in a money market mutual fund
D. A money market deposit account
Answer: C. Shares in a money market mutual fund
FDIC covers cash and cash-equivalents including CDs and deposit accounts, but not securities or money market mutual funds.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ A certificate of deposit (CD) — A CD is a deposit product fully covered by FDIC insurance.
✗ A savings account — A savings account is a deposit account covered by FDIC insurance.
✗ A money market deposit account — A money market DEPOSIT account is FDIC-insured; a money market MUTUAL FUND (a security) is not.

——————————
[Q 3 / 17 · Bank regulators]
Which agency conducts monetary policy?
A. OCC
B. FDIC
C. Federal Reserve Board
D. NCUA
Answer: C. Federal Reserve Board
The Federal Reserve Board conducts monetary policy. The OCC charters national banks and the FDIC insures deposits.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ OCC — The OCC charters and supervises national banks; it does not conduct monetary policy.
✗ FDIC — The FDIC insures bank deposits; monetary policy is the Federal Reserve's role.
✗ NCUA — The NCUA insures/regulates credit unions; it does not set monetary policy.

——————————
[Q 4 / 17 · Net worth equation]
On the statement of financial position, net worth equals:
A. Assets + Liabilities
B. Assets − Liabilities
C. Income − Expenses
D. Liabilities − Assets
Answer: B. Assets − Liabilities
Assets = Liabilities + Net Worth, so Net Worth = Assets − Liabilities.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Assets + Liabilities — Confuses the accounting identity; assets equal liabilities PLUS net worth, so you subtract liabilities.
✗ Income − Expenses — That is net cash flow from the cash flow statement, not net worth from the balance sheet.
✗ Liabilities − Assets — Reversed; subtracting assets from liabilities gives a negative of net worth. It is Assets minus Liabilities.

——————————
[Q 5 / 17 · Asset valuation]
At what value are assets reported on a personal statement of financial position?
A. Original purchase cost
B. Fair market value (FMV)
C. FMV net of any early-withdrawal penalties
D. Tax basis
Answer: B. Fair market value (FMV)
Assets are reported at fair market value. FMV is used even when an asset is subject to an early-withdrawal penalty; the penalty is ignored.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Original purchase cost — That is historical cost/basis; personal balance sheets use current fair market value.
✗ FMV net of any early-withdrawal penalties — FMV is used and penalties are ignored; you do not net them out.
✗ Tax basis — Tax basis is used for gain/loss calculations, not for reporting asset value on the statement of financial position.

——————————
[Q 6 / 17 · Liability measurement]
How is a mortgage reported on the statement of financial position?
A. At its original loan amount
B. At the monthly payment amount
C. At the outstanding principal balance
D. At principal plus all remaining interest
Answer: C. At the outstanding principal balance
Liabilities are listed at the outstanding principal balance — not the original amount, the payment, or principal plus future interest.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ At its original loan amount — The original amount ignores principal already repaid; report the current outstanding balance.
✗ At the monthly payment amount — The payment is a cash-flow item, not the balance-sheet liability value.
✗ At principal plus all remaining interest — Future interest is not yet owed as a liability; only the outstanding principal is listed.

——————————
[Q 7 / 17 · Housing ratio]
A client's monthly PITI is $2,000 and gross monthly income is $8,000. The housing (front-end) ratio is and:
A. 25%, within the 28% benchmark
B. 25%, exceeds the 28% benchmark
C. 16.7%, uses net income
D. 40%, exceeds the benchmark
Answer: A. 25%, within the 28% benchmark
$2,000 / $8,000 = 25% of gross income, within the ≤ 28% benchmark. The housing ratio uses gross income.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 25%, exceeds the 28% benchmark — 25% is within, not above, the 28% front-end benchmark.
✗ 16.7%, uses net income — The ratio uses gross income; $2,000/$8,000 = 25%, not 16.7%.
✗ 40%, exceeds the benchmark — Miscalculated; $2,000/$8,000 is 25%, and it does not exceed 28%.

——————————
[Q 8 / 17 · Total debt ratio]
The total (back-end) debt ratio benchmark is and is measured against income.
A. 28%; net
B. 36%; gross
C. 20%; net
D. 43%; gross
Answer: B. 36%; gross
The total debt ratio should be ≤ 36% of gross monthly income, including housing plus consumer debt and support obligations.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 28%; net — 28% is the front-end (housing) benchmark, and the debt ratios use gross, not net, income.
✗ 20%; net — 20% net is the consumer-debt benchmark, not the total back-end ratio.
✗ 43%; gross — 43% is a qualified-mortgage lending threshold, not the standard 36% back-end planning benchmark.

——————————
[Q 9 / 17 · Consumer debt ratio]
The consumer (non-mortgage) debt ratio benchmark of 20% is measured against which income figure?
A. Gross monthly income
B. Net monthly income (gross minus taxes)
C. Adjusted gross income
D. Taxable income
Answer: B. Net monthly income (gross minus taxes)
Consumer debt payments should be ≤ 20% of net monthly income; net is used because consumer debt interest is not tax-favored.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Gross monthly income — The housing and total-debt ratios use gross; the consumer-debt ratio uses net monthly income.
✗ Adjusted gross income — AGI is a tax concept; the consumer-debt ratio is measured against net monthly income.
✗ Taxable income — Taxable income is a tax figure; the 20% consumer-debt benchmark uses net monthly income.

——————————
[Q 10 / 17 · Emergency fund 6 months]
For which client is a 6-month emergency fund most appropriate?
A. Married couple, both employed at stable jobs
B. Single wage earner with no other income source
C. Married couple with a large second income available
D. Dual-income household with substantial liquid assets
Answer: B. Single wage earner with no other income source
Six months is appropriate for a single wage earner or a married couple with only one spouse employed; three months suits dual-income or second-income situations.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Married couple, both employed at stable jobs — Dual stable incomes support a 3-month fund; six months is for single-earner situations.
✗ Married couple with a large second income available — A second income cushions job loss, so three months suffices, not six.
✗ Dual-income household with substantial liquid assets — Two incomes plus ample liquidity call for three months, not six.

——————————
[Q 11 / 17 · Net investment ratio]
The net-investment-assets-to-net-worth ratio is generally considered adequate when it is at least:
A. 10%
B. 20%
C. 50%
D. 100%
Answer: C. 50%
This ratio (excluding home equity) should be ≥ 50% and rising toward retirement; younger clients are often around 20% or less.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 10% — Too low; the target is at least 50%, though younger clients may start near 20% or less.
✗ 20% — 20% is typical for younger clients, not the 'adequate' benchmark, which is at least 50%.
✗ 100% — Overstated; the ratio need only reach at least 50% and rise toward retirement, not 100%.

——————————
[Q 12 / 17 · Savings ratio]
Regarding the recommended savings ratio of at least 10% of gross income, employer qualified-plan contributions:
A. Do not count at all
B. Count toward the savings ratio
C. Count only if vested
D. Are counted as income, not savings
Answer: B. Count toward the savings ratio
Employer contributions to qualified plans count toward the recommended savings ratio of at least 10% of gross income.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Do not count at all — Employer qualified-plan contributions DO count toward the 10% savings ratio.
✗ Count only if vested — Vesting is irrelevant here; employer contributions count toward the savings ratio regardless.
✗ Are counted as income, not savings — Employer plan contributions are treated as savings, not as current income, for this ratio.

——————————
[Q 13 / 17 · Debt payoff]
A client paying off the smallest balances first to build motivation is using the:
A. Avalanche technique
B. Snowball technique
C. Refinancing technique
D. Amortization technique
Answer: B. Snowball technique
The snowball technique targets the smallest balances first for motivation; the avalanche technique targets the highest-interest debt first to save money.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Avalanche technique — The avalanche targets the highest-interest debt first to minimize interest, not the smallest balance.
✗ Refinancing technique — Refinancing replaces a loan with better terms; it is not a debt-payoff ordering method.
✗ Amortization technique — Amortization is the scheduled paydown of a loan, not a motivational payoff strategy.

——————————
[Q 14 / 17 · FICO weighting]
Which factor carries the greatest weight in a FICO score?
A. Length of credit history (15%)
B. Amounts owed / utilization (30%)
C. Payment history (35%)
D. New credit (10%)
Answer: C. Payment history (35%)
Payment history is the most heavily weighted factor at 35%, followed by amounts owed at 30%.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Length of credit history (15%) — At 15% it is a minor factor; payment history (35%) carries the greatest weight.
✗ Amounts owed / utilization (30%) — At 30% it is the second-largest factor, behind payment history at 35%.
✗ New credit (10%) — At only 10%, new credit is among the smallest FICO factors.

——————————
[Q 15 / 17 · Mortgage point]
One mortgage point equals:
A. 1% of the home's value
B. 1% of the amount borrowed
C. $1,000 regardless of loan size
D. 1% of the monthly payment
Answer: B. 1% of the amount borrowed
A point equals 1% of the amount borrowed, paid up front to obtain a lower interest rate.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 1% of the home's value — A point is based on the loan amount borrowed, not the home's value or price.
✗ $1,000 regardless of loan size — A point is 1% of the loan, so its dollar amount varies with loan size, not a flat $1,000.
✗ 1% of the monthly payment — A point is 1% of the amount borrowed, not of the monthly payment.

——————————
[Q 16 / 17 · VA loan]
Which is true of a VA loan?
A. Requires at least 3.5% down
B. Requires PMI when down payment is under 20%
C. Can be obtained with no down payment and no PMI
D. Is only available for jumbo amounts
Answer: C. Can be obtained with no down payment and no PMI
VA loans can be obtained with no down payment and require no PMI, though they charge a funding fee. FHA loans require a 3.5% minimum down payment.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Requires at least 3.5% down — The 3.5% minimum down payment applies to FHA loans; VA loans allow zero down.
✗ Requires PMI when down payment is under 20% — VA loans never require PMI; they charge a funding fee instead.
✗ Is only available for jumbo amounts — VA loans are for eligible veterans and are not restricted to jumbo loan amounts.

——————————
[Q 17 / 17 · Reverse mortgage age]
What is the minimum age to obtain a reverse (home equity conversion) mortgage?
A. 55
B. 59½
C. 62
D. 65
Answer: C. 62
A borrower must be age 62 or older. The lender pays the homeowner, and the loan is nonrecourse.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ 55 — Too young; the HECM minimum is age 62.
✗ 59½ — 59½ is the retirement-account penalty age, not the reverse-mortgage minimum of 62.
✗ 65 — The minimum is 62, not 65.



===== FP511 · M4 TIME VALUE OF MONEY =====

[4 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 4 · Ordinary vs due]
Lease payments and education/retirement funding contributions made at the beginning of each period are an example of a(n):
A. Ordinary annuity
B. Annuity due
C. Perpetuity
D. Lump sum
Answer: B. Annuity due
Payments at the beginning of each period form an annuity due (leases, funding goals). Ordinary annuities (e.g., mortgages) pay at period-end.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Ordinary annuity — Ordinary annuities pay at period-END (e.g., mortgages); beginning-of-period payments are an annuity due.
✗ Perpetuity — A perpetuity pays forever with no end; these are finite, timing-specific payments.
✗ Lump sum — A lump sum is a single payment, not a series of beginning-of-period payments.

——————————
[Q 2 / 4 · Real rate]
Compared with simply subtracting inflation from the rate of return, the correctly computed inflation-adjusted (real) rate is:
A. Always slightly higher
B. Always slightly lower
C. Exactly equal
D. Unrelated
Answer: B. Always slightly lower
The inflation-adjusted rate from [(1+return)/(1+inflation) − 1] × 100 is always slightly less than (return − inflation).
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Always slightly higher — The correct real rate from the Fisher formula is slightly LOWER than return minus inflation, not higher.
✗ Exactly equal — Only approximately equal; the compounding in the true formula makes it slightly lower.
✗ Unrelated — They are closely related; the correct method just yields a slightly lower figure.

——————————
[Q 3 / 4 · NPV rule]
If an investment has a negative net present value (NPV), then its return is:
A. Greater than the discount rate
B. Equal to the discount rate
C. Less than the discount rate
D. Equal to zero
Answer: C. Less than the discount rate
A negative NPV means the return is less than the discount (required) rate; a positive NPV means the return exceeds it.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Greater than the discount rate — A return above the discount rate produces a POSITIVE NPV, not a negative one.
✗ Equal to the discount rate — When return equals the discount rate, NPV is zero, not negative.
✗ Equal to zero — A zero return is unrelated to NPV sign; negative NPV means return is below the discount rate.

——————————
[Q 4 / 4 · Serial payment]
Compared with a level (fixed) annuity payment funding the same goal, the FIRST serial payment is:
A. Larger than the fixed payment
B. Smaller than the fixed payment
C. Identical to the fixed payment
D. Zero
Answer: B. Smaller than the fixed payment
A serial payment grows with inflation, so the first serial payment is smaller than the equivalent fixed payment and the last is larger.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Larger than the fixed payment — Reversed; serial payments start smaller and grow, so the first is smaller, not larger.
✗ Identical to the fixed payment — Serial payments rise with inflation, so they are not equal to the level payment.
✗ Zero — The first serial payment is a real, positive amount, just smaller than the fixed one, not zero.



===== FP511 · M5 PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT & FIDUCIARY =====

[8 questions]

——————————
[Q 1 / 8 · Fiduciary Duty]
Under Standard A.1, the Fiduciary Duty owed when providing Financial Advice consists of which three duties?
A. Loyalty, Care, and Follow Client Instructions
B. Integrity, Competence, and Diligence
C. Disclosure, Consent, and Management
D. Loyalty, Confidentiality, and Professionalism
Answer: A. Loyalty, Care, and Follow Client Instructions
The Fiduciary Duty is composed of the Duty of Loyalty, the Duty of Care, and the Duty to Follow Client Instructions.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Integrity, Competence, and Diligence — These are separate standalone standards (A.2–A.4 area), not the three A.1 fiduciary duties.
✗ Disclosure, Consent, and Management — That's the conflict-of-interest process (A.5), not the fiduciary duty's three components.
✗ Loyalty, Confidentiality, and Professionalism — Only Loyalty belongs; Confidentiality (A.9) and Professionalism are separate standards, not fiduciary duties.

——————————
[Q 2 / 8 · Conflicts of interest]
A CFP® professional sincerely believes a recommendation is in the client's best interest despite a related compensation conflict. Under Standard A.5, the conflict must be:
A. Disclosed only if the client asks
B. Ignored because the planner is acting in the client's best interest
C. Disclosed even though the planner believes she is acting in the client's best interest
D. Disclosed only after implementation
Answer: C. Disclosed even though the planner believes she is acting in the client's best interest
A material conflict of interest must be disclosed even if the CFP® professional believes she is acting in the client's best interest; she must also obtain informed consent and manage the conflict.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Disclosed only if the client asks — Disclosure is mandatory and proactive; it is not contingent on the client asking.
✗ Ignored because the planner is acting in the client's best interest — A sincere best-interest belief does NOT excuse disclosure — material conflicts must still be disclosed and managed.
✗ Disclosed only after implementation — Disclosure and informed consent must come before/at recommendation, not after implementation.

——————————
[Q 3 / 8 · Competence]
A CFP® professional is asked to provide a service for which she lacks sufficient competence. Standard A.3 permits all of the following responses EXCEPT:
A. Gain the necessary competence
B. Limit the scope of the engagement
C. Refer the client to a competent professional
D. Proceed and disclaim liability in the engagement letter
Answer: D. Proceed and disclaim liability in the engagement letter
Under Competence, the planner must gain competence, get a competent professional's help, limit scope, refer, and/or terminate — not simply proceed with a disclaimer.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Gain the necessary competence — Gaining competence is an explicitly permitted A.3 response, so it isn't the exception.
✗ Limit the scope of the engagement — Limiting scope to competent areas is a permitted A.3 response.
✗ Refer the client to a competent professional — Referring to a competent professional is permitted under A.3; proceeding with a disclaimer is not.

——————————
[Q 4 / 8 · Technology standard]
Under Standard A.14, when relying on technology to provide services, a CFP® professional must:
A. Be a technology expert
B. Have a reasonable basis for reliability, exercise reasonable care, and have a reasonable understanding
C. Avoid all third-party software
D. Personally audit the source code
Answer: B. Have a reasonable basis for reliability, exercise reasonable care, and have a reasonable understanding
Standard A.14 requires a reasonable basis for reliability, reasonable care, and a reasonable understanding — the professional is not required to be an expert.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Be a technology expert — A.14 requires only reasonable understanding, not expert-level technical mastery.
✗ Avoid all third-party software — A.14 permits reliance on technology; it doesn't ban third-party software.
✗ Personally audit the source code — Reasonable diligence is required, not a personal source-code audit.

——————————
[Q 5 / 8 · Recommending others]
When recommending another professional to a client, Standard A.13 requires the CFP® professional to do all of the following EXCEPT:
A. Have a reasonable basis for the referral
B. Disclose compensation paid by anyone other than the client
C. Guarantee the other professional's performance
D. Communicate the respective roles and inform the client of non-performance
Answer: C. Guarantee the other professional's performance
A.13 requires a reasonable basis, disclosure of referral compensation, communication of roles, and informing the client of non-performance — not a guarantee of the other party's work.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Have a reasonable basis for the referral — A reasonable basis IS required by A.13, so it is not the exception.
✗ Disclose compensation paid by anyone other than the client — Disclosing third-party referral compensation is required by A.13.
✗ Communicate the respective roles and inform the client of non-performance — Communicating roles and reporting non-performance are A.13 requirements; guaranteeing performance is not.

——————————
[Q 6 / 8 · Purpose of Code]
Which is NOT one of the three stated purposes of the Code of Ethics and Standards of Conduct?
A. Benefit and protect the public
B. Provide standards for delivering financial planning
C. Advance financial planning as a distinct and valuable profession
D. Maximize CFP® professionals' compensation
Answer: D. Maximize CFP® professionals' compensation
The three purposes are to benefit/protect the public, provide standards, and advance the profession. Maximizing compensation is not a stated purpose.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Benefit and protect the public — This IS one of the three stated purposes, so it isn't the exception.
✗ Provide standards for delivering financial planning — Providing delivery standards is a stated purpose of the Code.
✗ Advance financial planning as a distinct and valuable profession — Advancing the profession is a stated purpose; maximizing compensation is not.

——————————
[Q 7 / 8 · Confidentiality exceptions]
Standard A.9 permits use or disclosure of confidential client information for which two purposes?
A. Marketing and recruiting
B. Ordinary business use and legal/compliance purposes
C. Tax filing and social media
D. Referral solicitation and advertising
Answer: B. Ordinary business use and legal/compliance purposes
The two exceptions to confidentiality are ordinary business use and legal/compliance purposes.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Marketing and recruiting — Marketing and recruiting are not A.9 confidentiality exceptions — only ordinary business and legal/compliance use.
✗ Tax filing and social media — Social media disclosure is never permitted; the exceptions are ordinary business and legal/compliance use.
✗ Referral solicitation and advertising — Advertising/solicitation are not confidentiality exceptions under A.9.

——————————
[Q 8 / 8 · Dealer markup]
A securities firm trades from its own account and charges clients the difference between the interdealer offer price and the price it charges. This compensation is a:
A. Commission
B. Markup
C. Advisory fee
D. Loaded sales charge
Answer: B. Markup
A dealer/principal trading from its own account (position trading) charges a markup. A broker/agent arranging trades charges a commission.
[Why the others are wrong:]
✗ Commission — A commission is charged by a broker/agent ARRANGING a trade, not a dealer trading from its own inventory.
✗ Advisory fee — An advisory fee compensates ongoing advice, not a principal trade spread.
✗ Loaded sales charge — A sales load applies to mutual fund purchases, not to a dealer's principal-trade markup.
